title: Selling a Share of Your Deal Is Selling a Security
summary: When you take money from passive investors in return for a share of a project's profit, you are usually selling a security, and securities law applies before the first conversation. This lesson explains what makes an interest a security, why the default is a full prospectus, and how exemptions and marketing limits work in concept.
body:
The moment you offer people a share of a project's profit, in return for money, while you do the work, you are very likely selling a security. Securities law then governs who you may approach, what you may say and what you must give them, before a single dollar moves.

Recall

Q. What is a shotgun clause?

A. A buy-sell clause in which one partner names a price for the whole equity and the other must either buy or sell at that price.

Q. In a joint venture, what do major decision rights protect?

A. The non-managing partner's ability to block decisions that change the risk of its investment, such as a sale, refinancing, a new budget or a change of business plan.

Q. In indirect tax, what is the difference between an exempt and a zero-rated supply, in general terms?

A. In many value-added tax systems, a zero-rated supply is taxable at a rate of zero, so input tax can usually be recovered; an exempt supply is outside the tax, so input tax usually cannot. Treatment varies; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the first time you raise equity from people outside your own balance sheet, you will feel that you are simply asking friends or contacts to join a good deal. The law usually sees it differently. It sees an issuer selling investment interests to the public, and it exists to protect those buyers. Breaking securities rules can give investors the right to demand their money back, can bring regulatory penalties, and can make lenders and later investors refuse to deal with you. The rules are technical and vary by jurisdiction, so this week is concepts, not conclusions. Every real raise needs securities counsel before it starts.

What makes something a security

In plain English: if people give you money, expecting a profit, and the profit depends mainly on your work rather than theirs, the arrangement is probably a security, whatever you call it.

A security is a financial interest that the law regulates because buyers depend on others for their return. Shares and bonds are obvious examples. The harder category is the investment contract, which courts in the United States and Canada have defined broadly. In the United States, the Supreme Court's 1946 decision in SEC v. W.J. Howey Co. described it, in substance, as an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profits from the efforts of others. The Supreme Court of Canada took a similar approach in Pacific Coast Coin Exchange of Canada v. Ontario Securities Commission in 1978. The labels on your documents do not decide the question; the economic reality does.

Worked example one, hypothetical. You form a limited partnership to build a 30-unit building. Twelve people each contribute 250,000 dollars as limited partners. You, as general partner, find the site, manage design, hire the contractor and run lease-up. The limited partners vote only on a sale. That is a textbook security: money in, a common enterprise, profit expected from your efforts.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Two experienced developers each put in 2,000,000 dollars, share every major decision, each supervise half of the work, and each can veto the budget. The interests may not be securities, because each partner's profit depends substantially on its own efforts and control. But this is fact-specific, and the line is not always clear. Treat the question as one for counsel, not for instinct.

Say that out loud now.

Money in, common enterprise, profit from my efforts: that is a security, whatever I call it.

The default rule and the exemptions

The default rule in most securities regimes is that an issuer may sell securities to the public only with a prospectus: a detailed disclosure document reviewed by the regulator, with legal liability attached to its contents. A prospectus is expensive and slow, and few small real estate projects use one.

Instead, most private real estate raises rely on a prospectus exemption: a rule that lets an issuer sell securities without a prospectus to certain buyers, in certain amounts, or with certain disclosure, on conditions. Common categories, described conceptually, include sales to investors who meet a financial or professional test, often called accredited investors; sales to a small circle of people with a close existing relationship to the issuer; sales above a minimum investment size; and sales with a prescribed offering document. Each category has its own definitions, limits, filings and resale restrictions, and they differ by jurisdiction. Never assume a category fits; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Marketing limits

The third concept is the limit on how you may find investors. Many regimes restrict general solicitation: advertising or broadly publicising an offering to people the issuer does not already know, through public posts, mass emails, seminars or media. Some exemptions forbid it outright; some permit it on extra conditions, such as taking further steps to confirm each investor's eligibility. A casual post about "an opportunity to invest in my next project" can be general solicitation, and it can destroy the exemption you were relying on for the whole raise. This course does not teach outreach. It teaches the rule: no communication about an investment until counsel has confirmed the exemption and the permitted channels.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax. The vehicle used to issue interests, a partnership, company or trust, decides how investors are taxed; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability. The issuer and often its directors and promoters carry liability for what is said. Banking. Lenders will ask how equity was raised and whether it can be clawed back. Governance. Passive investors need defined rights and reporting. Estate. Investor interests must be transferable on death within resale rules. Exit. Resale restrictions mean investors may not be able to sell easily, which shapes your exit and refinance plans.

Why the law protects passive buyers

It helps to understand the reason behind the rules, because the reason predicts how a regulator will read your facts. A passive investor cannot inspect the site, cannot check the contractor's invoices and cannot stop you making a bad decision. Everything he knows about the investment comes from you. The sponsor holds information the buyer does not, and the buyer's return depends on the sponsor's honesty and skill. Securities law exists to close that information gap: by requiring disclosure, by limiting who may be sold to without full disclosure, and by giving buyers remedies when the disclosure is wrong.

Read that way, each rule makes sense. An eligibility test assumes some investors can afford advisers and absorb a loss. A relationship test assumes people close to you already know you and the business. A marketing limit stops a private offering becoming a public one by the back door. When you are unsure whether a plan is acceptable, ask the question the regulator will ask: does this buyer have what he needs to judge the risk, and did he choose freely, without pressure or a misleading picture? If the honest answer is no, the plan is probably wrong, whatever the technical rule says.

This also explains why you cannot contract out of the rules. A clause in which investors agree that their interests are not securities, or waive their rights, does not change the economic reality the law looks at.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating an equity raise as a private conversation rather than a regulated sale, so the exemption fails after the money is in. The control is a written raise plan, approved by securities counsel before any outreach, naming the exemption, the eligible investors, the permitted channels and the documents.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks securities law applies only to big public companies. It applies to the smallest raise from three people, if they are passive and expect profit from your work.

Callback

In Week 38, JAX taught waterfalls and promotes. A waterfall is exactly the kind of profit-sharing promise securities law treats as an investment contract when the investors are passive. The economics you designed in Week 38 are the security you are regulated for this week.

Recap

Passive money in a common enterprise, expecting profit from your efforts, is usually a security. The default is a prospectus; private raises rely on exemptions with conditions; marketing limits can void an exemption. Counsel first, communication second. Professional sign-off required: securities lawyer, in each jurisdiction where an investor lives.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite raise that failed its exemption.
checklist: Are the investors passive, expecting profit mainly from my efforts?
Has securities counsel confirmed in writing whether the interests are securities?
Which exemption is relied on, and in which jurisdictions do investors live?
What are the eligibility tests, limits, filings and resale restrictions of that exemption?
Which communication channels are permitted, and is general solicitation allowed?
Is there a written raise plan approved before any outreach?
Do my documents and my words say the same thing?
head: Field checklist
speak: If I take money from passive people who expect a profit from my work, I am almost certainly selling a security, whatever the documents call it. The US Supreme Court described an investment contract in Howey in 1946 as money in a common enterprise with profit expected from the efforts of others, and the Supreme Court of Canada took a similar approach in Pacific Coast Coin Exchange in 1978. The default rule is that selling to the public needs a prospectus. Private raises instead rely on exemptions, such as sales to investors who meet a financial test, to a close circle, above a minimum size, or with a prescribed offering document, each with conditions that vary by jurisdiction. Many exemptions also restrict general solicitation, so a casual public post can void the exemption for the whole raise. So: counsel first, a written raise plan, then communication.
terms: Security — a financial interest regulated because its buyer depends on others for the return, including an investment contract.
Prospectus exemption — a rule that lets an issuer sell securities without a prospectus to defined buyers or on defined conditions.
General solicitation — advertising or broadly publicising an offering to people the issuer has no existing relationship with.

hostile.q: You say your investors are just partners in a joint venture. Why aren't their interests securities?
hostile.a: I do not assume they are not, and I have asked securities counsel to confirm in writing. If the investors are passive and expect profit from my efforts, I treat the interests as securities and rely on a confirmed exemption, with eligibility checks, required filings and no general solicitation. If counsel's view is that they are true joint venturers with real control, I will show you the governance terms that support that view.

title: The Raise That Lost Its Exemption
summary: This is a composite example of a small developer who raised equity through public posts and an informal pitch, relied on an exemption that did not fit, and faced rescission demands and regulatory action in the middle of construction. Cole assists on the legal reading.
body:
This is a composite example. A capable small developer raised equity the way he had seen others do it: a few posts, a pitch evening, a simple subscription form. The exemption he thought he had did not fit, and when construction hit trouble, the investors' right to their money back arrived at the worst possible moment.

Recall

Q. What is an investment contract, in the sense used by securities regulators?

A. In substance, an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profit from the efforts of others. Such interests are regulated as securities.

Q. What is a capital call remedy?

A. The consequence, written into a partnership agreement, for a partner who does not fund a valid call, such as a partner loan or dilution, usually after a cure period.

Q. Why are investment concessions often conditional?

A. Because a government grants them in exchange for outcomes such as investment, jobs or completion by a date. Missing a condition can reverse the benefit. The terms are set by the granting law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this failure began as a legal error and ended as a financial one. The developer did not intend to break any rule. He simply never asked, before he spoke to anyone, which rule he was raising under. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

Month 0: a developer plans a 24-unit building costing 9,000,000 dollars, with a 6,000,000 dollar construction loan and 3,000,000 dollars of equity. He has 600,000 dollars of his own and needs 2,400,000 dollars from investors. Month 1: he posts about the project on social media, describing "a chance to own part of a new building" with projected returns, and hosts an evening presentation for anyone interested. Month 2: 28 people subscribe, at minimums of 50,000 dollars, using a short form in which each ticks a box saying they qualify. Month 3: the loan closes. Month 12: costs rise and the first distribution date is pushed back. Month 14: several investors complain to the regulator. Month 16: the regulator finds that the exemption relied on did not permit public marketing and that several investors did not meet its eligibility test. Investors with a right to rescind demand their money back. The lender, told of the regulatory action, stops draws pending review.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Choosing an exemption from a template rather than from advice. Publicising the offering before confirming the permitted channels. And accepting self-certification by tick box, without checking that each investor actually met the test.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed that because the amounts were small, the rules were relaxed. He assumed a tick box shifted responsibility to the investor. He assumed that if everything went well, nobody would ever check. Cole's reading is that an issuer generally carries the burden of showing an exemption was available, and that the question is usually examined precisely when things go badly, because that is when investors look for a way out.

4. Incentives

The developer's incentive was speed: the land deadline was close. Investors' incentive, early on, was to secure a place in what looked like a good deal, so they ticked whatever box was needed. Later, when the project slipped, a rescission right was worth more to each investor than a delayed share of profit. The lender's incentive was to protect its loan from any claim that equity could be withdrawn. Every incentive moved against the developer once the project hit trouble.

Say that out loud now.

The exemption is tested when things go badly, by people who want their money back.

5. Warning signs ignored

A lawyer friend's comment that "you should get a securities lawyer to look at this" in month 0. Questions at the presentation from people who clearly did not understand real estate risk. The fact that the subscription form was copied from another developer's project in another jurisdiction. And the lender's term sheet, which asked for a confirmation that equity had been raised in compliance with securities law, signed without checking.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was month 1, the first public post. Before it, any exemption remained available to be chosen properly. After it, an exemption that forbade public marketing was likely gone for the whole raise, and the developer's remaining options depended on regulatory relief, a fresh offering, or buying investors out.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the cost overrun. Overruns happen. The root cause was raising money without first deciding, with counsel, which exemption applied and what it required. That turned an ordinary delay into a regulatory event and a contingent liability equal to much of the equity raised.

Cole's reading: the controls that were missing

Cole lists five. A written raise plan, signed off by securities counsel in each investor's jurisdiction, before any communication. A rule that no public channel is used unless the chosen exemption permits it. Verification of each investor's eligibility, with evidence on file rather than a tick box. An offering document that states the risks, including delay and loss, plainly. And a register of every person contacted, when and how, so the issuer can show that the channels used were permitted.

What a recovery would have looked like

Ford's question at any failure is always: what was the cheapest exit at each stage? In month 1, before the first post, the cost was a securities lawyer's fee and a slower start. In month 3, before the loan closed, the developer could still have paused, taken advice, offered the ineligible investors their money back voluntarily and replaced that equity, at the cost of delay and some embarrassment. By month 14, with the regulator involved and construction under way, every option was expensive: regulatory relief if available, a compliant re-offering to eligible investors, or buying out the investors who wanted to leave, funded by new equity on worse terms because the project was now visibly in trouble.

The pattern is the same one Ford has shown in every forensic case this course has studied. A defect that is cheap to fix before money moves becomes expensive once others rely on it, and ruinous once the project is under stress. Securities defects are especially harsh because they are invisible on site. Nothing about the building looks wrong. The problem lives in a subscription file nobody opens until somebody wants out.

Cole adds one more point. The developer's signed confirmation to the lender, that equity had been raised in compliance with securities law, was itself now a problem: a representation that was not true when made. A careful borrower signs that confirmation only with counsel's written view in hand.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a failed exemption creates a right to return of capital, which surfaces when the project is weakest. The control is to fix the exemption and channels with counsel first and to verify every investor's eligibility.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner copies a subscription form from another deal. Forms carry assumptions about jurisdiction, investor type and exemption. A form that worked elsewhere can be wrong for yours.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to use professionals: engagement letters, clear instructions and the discipline to ask before acting. This developer had a lawyer friend's warning and did not engage anyone. An engagement letter signed in month 0 would have cost a small fraction of what month 16 cost.

Recap

A public post, a tick-box form, ineligible investors and the wrong exemption: invisible while the project went well, decisive when it did not. Rescission demands and a lender freeze followed. The prevention is counsel, a plan and verification before the first word.

Rule 70: Never speak to anyone about investing in a project until securities counsel has confirmed in writing the exemption, the eligible investors, the permitted channels and the documents, and verify every investor's eligibility with evidence on file.

Next: Roman on The Money: what a failed exemption costs, priced as a contingent liability.
checklist: Has securities counsel confirmed the exemption in writing for each investor's jurisdiction?
Does the chosen exemption permit the channels I plan to use?
Is each investor's eligibility verified with evidence, not a tick box?
Is the subscription form drafted for this deal and this jurisdiction?
Does the offering document state delay and loss risks plainly?
Do I keep a register of every contact, date and channel?
Can I truthfully sign the lender's securities compliance confirmation?
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A developer needed 2,400,000 dollars of investor equity. He posted publicly about the project, held an open presentation, and took 28 subscriptions on a short form where investors ticked a box to say they qualified. When costs rose and distributions slipped, investors complained, the regulator found the exemption did not allow public marketing and several investors did not qualify, rescission demands followed, and the lender froze draws. The overrun was not the root cause. The root cause was raising money without first fixing, with counsel, which exemption applied and what it required. The point of no return was the first public post. Rule 70: never speak to anyone about investing until securities counsel has confirmed in writing the exemption, the eligible investors, the channels and the documents, and verify every investor's eligibility with evidence on file.
terms: Rescission — the unwinding of a purchase, so the buyer returns the security and receives back what it paid, sometimes with interest.
Self-certification — an investor's own statement that it meets an eligibility test, which on its own may not be enough to show the exemption applied.
Contact register — a record of every person approached about an offering, with date and channel, used to show the channels were permitted.

hostile.q: Your equity came from 28 people after public posts. How do I know they cannot demand their money back halfway through construction?
hostile.a: You should not rely on my word, and I would not either. I can give you securities counsel's written opinion on the exemption relied on, the evidence of each investor's eligibility, the contact register showing the channels used, and the filings made. If counsel identifies any gap, the plan is to cure it before closing, by a compliant re-offer or by buying those interests out, and to fund that from equity outside the project budget.

rule: Rule 70: Never speak to anyone about investing in a project until securities counsel has confirmed in writing the exemption, the eligible investors, the permitted channels and the documents, and verify every investor's eligibility with evidence on file.

title: What a Failed Exemption Costs
summary: A failed securities exemption is not a fine; it is a contingent liability that can equal the equity raised, and it surfaces when the project is weakest. This lesson prices it, compares it with the cost of compliance, and shows how it moves the lender's view and your return. Warrick's Wealth Ledger closes it.
body:
The cost of getting a raise wrong is not the regulator's penalty. It is the investors' right to their money back, which behaves like a put option you sold for nothing, exercisable when your project can least afford it.

Recall

Q. What is penalty dilution?

A. A dilution formula that credits the partner who funds a missed call with more than it paid, so the defaulting partner loses a larger share of eventual equity value.

Q. What reporting does a joint venture partner usually require?

A. Regular financial statements, budget against actual, the schedule, material events and approvals sought, delivered on a fixed timetable.

Q. In customs, what is the dutiable value of an import, in general terms?

A. Usually the transaction value of the goods, adjusted by rules on what costs to include. The rules vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers tend to treat securities compliance as an overhead to be minimised. A risk manager treats it as an insurance premium against one of the few liabilities that can unwind your equity. Today we price both sides: the premium, which is the cost of doing the raise properly, and the loss, which is what happens when it fails. All figures are hypothetical round numbers. Rescission rights, damages and penalties are set by law and vary by jurisdiction, so treat every mechanism here as a concept to confirm with counsel.

The contingent liability

In plain English: if investors have the right to hand back their interest and demand their money, that right is a debt that has not yet been called.

A contingent liability is an obligation that may arise depending on a future event. A failed exemption can create one, because investors may be entitled to rescission: return of the amount paid, sometimes with interest, in exchange for the security. Unlike a loan, this liability has no schedule. It is called when investors choose, and they choose when the project's value has fallen below what they paid.

Worked example one, hypothetical. You raise 3,000,000 dollars from 20 investors at 150,000 dollars each. Later, counsel finds that 6 of them did not qualify under the exemption. Assume, for illustration, that those 6 hold a rescission right with simple interest at 5 percent per year. Two years in, the claim is 6 times 150,000 dollars, which is 900,000 dollars of principal, plus 900,000 times 5 percent times 2, which is 90,000 dollars of interest. The contingent liability is 990,000 dollars. Now ask when it will be called. In year two the building is half complete and valued below cost. Every one of those 6 investors would rather have 165,000 dollars back than wait for a delayed and uncertain profit.

What it does to the deal

The liability has three effects. First, liquidity: 990,000 dollars must come from somewhere, and the project budget does not contain it. Second, the lender: a loan agreement commonly treats material litigation or regulatory action as an event of default, or at least a reason to stop funding, and a lender will not want equity it counted on being withdrawn. Third, everyone else's return: if the developer funds the rescission from his own pocket, his capital rises and his return falls; if the project funds it, the remaining investors are diluted or delayed.

Worked example two, hypothetical. The developer's own equity was 500,000 dollars, with a promote projected to bring his total return to 2,000,000 dollars on exit. Funding the 990,000 dollar rescission personally nearly triples his capital to 1,490,000 dollars, and if the promote is unchanged, his projected multiple falls from 4 times to about 1.3 times, before any regulatory penalty or legal cost.

Say that out loud now.

A failed exemption is a put option I sold for nothing, called when I am weakest.

The premium: the cost of doing it properly

Now price the premium. Assume securities counsel, investor verification, a proper offering document and filings cost 60,000 dollars for this raise. That is 2 percent of the 3,000,000 dollars raised. Compare it with an expected loss. If, without advice, you judge there is a one in four chance the exemption fails, and a failure costs at least 990,000 dollars plus legal costs, the expected loss is roughly 250,000 dollars or more. Even at much lower probabilities, the premium usually wins, because the loss lands at the worst moment and can trigger a loan default that multiplies it. A risk manager does not ask whether failure is likely. He asks whether the project survives it.

How the lender reads it

A construction lender sizes the loan on the assumption that the equity is permanent and first-loss. Equity subject to a rescission right is closer to a demand loan from investors, ranking ahead of the lender in practice if it is paid out. That is why loan agreements commonly ask for a confirmation that equity was raised lawfully, and why some lenders ask to see counsel's view. A clean raise is part of your credit.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, a raise you lead creates a hidden liability: your exposure if the exemption fails and you choose, or are required, to make investors whole. Record it as a contingent liability in your own ledger until counsel confirms the exemption and the resale and filing steps are complete. And never let personal guarantees, personal capital and an unverified raise stack on the same project. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Penalties and the reputation cost

Beyond rescission, a regulator may impose sanctions such as administrative penalties, orders restricting future fundraising, or bans on acting as a director or promoter, depending on the regime and the seriousness of the breach; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Those are hard to price, but the reputational cost is easier to see. Many lenders and institutional investors ask, in their due diligence, whether the sponsor or its principals have ever been subject to regulatory proceedings. A yes does not end every conversation, but it adds months of questions and can close the doors to the cheapest capital.

Treat that as a cost of capital. If a clean record lets you borrow or raise at even a small spread better than a sponsor with a mark against him, across a career of projects that spread compounds into a very large sum. The 60,000 dollar compliance premium on one raise is a payment that protects the price of every raise after it.

What disciplined sponsors do

Well-run sponsors budget compliance as a fixed line in sources and uses, not as a discretionary legal fee, and they will not let a raise launch until a named person has signed off that the exemption analysis, investor verification process and filing calendar are complete. A small developer can copy both: a compliance line in every pro forma and a sign-off before launch.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a defective raise turns the equity cushion into a demand liability exactly when the project is under pressure. The control is to spend the compliance premium up front and to obtain counsel's written view before closing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares the compliance cost with zero. The right comparison is with the expected cost of rescission, a lender freeze and lost reputation, weighted by when it would arrive.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught stress tests and severe cases that combine several shocks. A failed exemption is one of those combining shocks: it arrives with the cost overrun, not instead of it, because the overrun is what makes investors want out.

Recap

A failed exemption can create a rescission right that behaves like a contingent demand liability. It hits liquidity, the loan and every party's return at once. The compliance premium is usually small against the expected loss. Price both, and spend the premium.

Next: REGA on The Rules: the tests regulators use, exemption conditions and resale limits.
checklist: Have I priced the rescission exposure if any investor did not qualify?
Have I estimated when that exposure would most likely be called?
Would a regulatory action be an event of default under the loan?
Have I budgeted the compliance premium before the raise?
Has counsel given a written view on the exemption before closing?
Is any rescission exposure recorded in my personal ledger until it is cleared?
Have I avoided stacking guarantees, personal capital and an unverified raise on one project?
head: Field checklist
speak: A failed securities exemption is priced as a contingent liability. Hypothetically, if 6 investors who paid 150,000 dollars each did not qualify and hold a right to rescind with 5 percent interest, after two years the claim is 990,000 dollars. It is called when the project is weakest, because that is when investors prefer their money back. It drains liquidity, can trigger a loan default or freeze, and dilutes everyone else's return; funded personally, it can cut a sponsor's projected multiple from 4 times to about 1.3 times. Against that, doing the raise properly might cost 2 percent of the equity. The question is not whether failure is likely but whether the project survives it. Lenders treat equity subject to rescission as closer to demand debt, so a clean raise is part of my credit. Personally, I record the exposure until counsel confirms the exemption.
terms: Contingent liability — an obligation that may arise depending on a future event, such as investors exercising a rescission right.
Expected loss — the size of a loss multiplied by its probability, used to compare a risk with the cost of preventing it.
First-loss equity — capital that absorbs losses before the lender, which is why lenders need it to be permanent.

hostile.q: How do I know your equity is permanent and not something your investors can withdraw?
hostile.a: Here is counsel's written view on the exemption relied on, the evidence of each investor's eligibility and the filings made. The offering documents give investors no redemption right, and the partnership agreement restricts transfers. If any gap is identified, I will cure it before closing from capital outside the project budget, so the equity you size the loan on is first-loss and cannot be called back.

title: The Tests Regulators Use: Security, Exemption, Resale
summary: Regulators ask three questions about a private raise: is this a security, which exemption applies and were its conditions met, and can the buyer resell. This lesson explains each test conceptually, including how investor eligibility, filings and hold periods work, without stating any jurisdiction's thresholds.
body:
A regulator looking at your raise asks three questions in order. Is it a security? If so, which exemption did you rely on, and did you meet every condition? And what limits apply when your investors want to sell?

Recall

Q. Why does a failed exemption behave like a contingent liability?

A. Because it can give investors a right to return of their money, which is called when the project is weakest and investors prefer cash to a delayed profit.

Q. In a joint venture, how is alignment between sponsor and investor usually created?

A. By sponsor co-investment, a promote paid only after investors clear hurdles, reasonable fees, and clear rules on related-party dealings.

Q. What is a stabilisation clause in an investment agreement with a government?

A. A promise that certain laws or terms affecting the investment will not change for a period, or that the investor will be compensated if they do. Enforceability varies; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will not be the one applying these tests, your securities counsel will. But you need to understand them well enough to give counsel the right facts, to spot when a plan drifts out of bounds, and to explain to a lender or investor why your raise is clean. This lesson is conceptual and names no threshold, rate or section. Every number in an exemption must come from counsel and the current rules, and you should verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Test one: is it a security?

Regulators apply a substance test, not a label test. The investment contract analysis from the United States case SEC v. W.J. Howey Co., decided in 1946, asks in substance whether there is an investment of money, in a common enterprise, with an expectation of profit from the efforts of others. The Supreme Court of Canada, in Pacific Coast Coin Exchange in 1978, adopted a broadly similar approach that focuses on whether the investor's return depends on the promoter's efforts. Both courts emphasised economic reality over form.

In real estate, the facts that point toward a security are passive investors, pooled money, a sponsor who controls the project and promised returns. The facts that point away are active co-owners who share control and work. Selling a whole building to one buyer for its own use is normally not a securities sale. Selling fractional interests in a building that you will manage and lease usually is.

Test two: which exemption, and were its conditions met?

An exemption is a set of conditions, and every condition matters. Conceptually, the main categories are these. An eligibility exemption lets you sell to investors who meet a financial or professional test, sometimes called accredited investors; the condition is that each buyer truly meets it, and the issuer usually needs a reasonable basis for believing so. A relationship exemption allows sales to a limited circle with a close existing connection to the issuer; the condition is that the connection is real and close, not invented for the deal. A minimum amount exemption allows sales above a set size, on the theory that large buyers can protect themselves; some regimes limit or restrict its use with individuals. An offering document exemption permits wider sales if a prescribed disclosure document is delivered and statutory rights attach to it.

Most exemptions also carry procedural conditions: a report or notice filed with the regulator within a set time, sometimes a fee, sometimes a risk acknowledgement signed by the investor, and limits on marketing. Missing a procedural step can be as damaging as selling to an ineligible buyer.

Say that out loud now.

An exemption is a list of conditions, and I must be able to prove every one.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A sponsor sells interests to 10 people. Seven meet an eligibility test with documents on file. Three are long-time colleagues who do not meet it, and the sponsor relies on a relationship exemption for them. Counsel confirms both exemptions are available in the investors' jurisdiction, that they can be combined, that a filing is due within the required period, and that no public marketing was used. The raise is clean because each investor is placed under a specific exemption, with evidence.

Test three: can the buyer resell?

Securities bought under a private exemption are commonly subject to resale restrictions: a hold period during which they cannot be freely sold to the public, or a requirement that any resale also fit an exemption. The rationale is to stop exemptions being used as a back door to public distribution. For you, resale restrictions matter in three ways. Investors must be told, plainly, that they may not be able to sell. Your own exit plan cannot assume a liquid market for the interests. And a transfer on death or divorce must be handled within the rules.

Worked example two, hypothetical. An investor who bought a 200,000 dollar interest wants to sell it two years later to a neighbour who is not eligible. Even if your partnership agreement allows transfers with consent, securities law may not allow that sale. The practical answer is often a buyback right in the partnership agreement, or a sale to an eligible buyer, both checked by counsel.

Multi-jurisdiction raises

Securities law usually applies where the investor is, not only where the issuer is. An investor who lives in another province, state or country can bring another regulator's rules into your raise. Map every investor's location before accepting them, and ask counsel which rules apply in each.

Professional sign-off required: securities lawyer, in each jurisdiction where an investor lives.

The record you must keep

Because the issuer usually carries the burden of showing an exemption applied, the file you keep is your defence. For each investor it should hold, at minimum: identity and jurisdiction, the exemption relied on, the evidence supporting eligibility or relationship, any signed risk acknowledgement, the subscription agreement, the date funds were received and the date of any filing. For the raise as a whole it should hold counsel's analysis, the offering document and every version of it, the contact register showing how and when each investor was approached, and copies of every filing and fee receipt.

Vera's rule from Week 82 applies here in advance: records made at the time are worth far more than records reconstructed later. A file assembled after a complaint looks like what it is. Build the file as the raise happens, investor by investor, and have someone other than the person selling check that each file is complete before funds are accepted.

A practical point on timing: some exemptions require the filing within a short period after the sale, and some require evidence of eligibility before the sale, not after. Missing the order can matter as much as missing the step. Put each date in a diary the day counsel gives it to you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on an exemption whose conditions you cannot prove, especially investor eligibility and filing deadlines. The control is to place every investor under a named exemption, keep the evidence, diary the filings and have counsel confirm the whole.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks one exemption covers the whole raise automatically. Each investor, in each jurisdiction, must fit an exemption, and the evidence must be kept investor by investor.

Callback

In Week 63, REGA and Omar taught foreign investment registration and know-your-client checks on money crossing borders. Securities rules follow the same logic: the rules of the investor's home matter, and the evidence must be collected at intake, not reconstructed later.

Recap

First, is it a security, judged by substance? Second, which exemption applies to each investor, and can you prove every condition, including filings and marketing limits? Third, what resale restrictions apply, and have investors been told? Counsel applies the tests; you supply the facts and the evidence.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: reverse engineering a raise from its finished size.
checklist: Have I described the investors' role and control honestly to counsel?
Is each investor placed under a named exemption, with evidence on file?
Have I mapped where every investor lives and which rules apply there?
Are filing deadlines and any fees diarised?
Has a risk acknowledgement been obtained where required?
Have investors been told plainly about resale restrictions?
Does my exit plan avoid assuming a liquid market for the interests?
head: Field checklist
speak: Regulators ask three questions. First, is it a security? That is judged by substance: Howey in the US in 1946 and Pacific Coast Coin Exchange in Canada in 1978 both look at money invested in a common enterprise with profit expected from the promoter's efforts. Passive pooled investors with a managing sponsor point to a security. Second, which exemption applies, and can I prove every condition? Categories include eligibility tests, close relationships, minimum amounts and prescribed offering documents, with procedural steps such as filings, risk acknowledgements and marketing limits. Every investor must fit a named exemption, with evidence. Third, can the buyer resell? Private securities usually carry hold periods or need another exemption for resale, so investors must be told and my exit cannot assume liquidity. The rules usually follow the investor's location, so I map every investor's jurisdiction and let counsel apply the tests.
terms: Investment contract test — the substance test courts use to decide whether an arrangement is a security, focused on profit from others' efforts.
Accredited investor — a conceptual label for an investor who meets a financial or professional test that permits sales without a prospectus.
Resale restriction — a limit on reselling privately issued securities, such as a hold period or a requirement that the resale fit an exemption.

hostile.q: Three of your investors don't meet the eligibility test. Which exemption covers them, and can you prove it?
hostile.a: Counsel placed those three under a relationship exemption because each has a long, documented working relationship with me, which we have recorded investor by investor. Counsel confirmed that exemption is available where they live and can be combined with the eligibility exemption. The filing was made within the required period, no public marketing was used, and I can give you counsel's letter and the evidence file.

title: Reverse Engineering a Raise From Its Finished Size
summary: Starting from a finished equity raise, this worked calculation works backward to the number of investors needed, the split between exemption categories, the compliance budget and the timeline to closing. All exemption limits are hypothetical, used only to show the method.
body:
Every raise has a finished size. Work backward from it, through the exemption's limits, to the number and type of investors, the cost and the calendar, and you will know before you start whether the raise can be done lawfully in the time you have.

Recall

Q. What three questions does a regulator ask about a private raise?

A. Is it a security? Which exemption applies to each investor, and were its conditions met? What resale restrictions apply?

Q. How does a sponsor's co-investment help alignment in a joint venture?

A. It puts the sponsor's own money at risk alongside investors, so the sponsor shares losses as well as the promote.

Q. What does know your client mean in banking?

A. The process of verifying a customer's identity, ownership and source of funds before and during the relationship, required by anti-money-laundering rules.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers usually start a raise from the front: here is my deal, let me see who is interested. Then they discover, halfway through, that the people interested do not fit the exemption, or that the filings and verification take longer than the land deadline allows. Reverse engineering starts from the end. This lesson uses an invented exemption regime with hypothetical limits, chosen only to show the method. Real limits must come from counsel and the current rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Step 1: the finished outcome

The project costs 15,000,000 dollars. The construction lender will lend 65 percent of cost, which is 9,750,000 dollars. Equity required is 15,000,000 less 9,750,000, which is 5,250,000 dollars. You and your partner will put in 750,000 dollars of your own. The raise must therefore produce 5,250,000 less 750,000, which is 4,500,000 dollars from investors, and the lender requires all equity in before the first draw, 120 days from today.

Step 2: the hypothetical exemption limits

Suppose counsel tells you, for this illustration only, that your investors' jurisdiction allows two routes. Route E, eligible investors, has no cap on amount or number but requires evidence that each investor meets the financial test. Route R, close relationships, allows at most 10 investors and at most 50,000 dollars each. Neither route allows public marketing.

Step 3: the most route R can carry

Route R is capped at 10 investors times 50,000 dollars, which is 500,000 dollars. Even if you fill it completely, route E must carry 4,500,000 less 500,000, which is 4,000,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

The capped route sets a ceiling, and the rest must come from investors who qualify.

Step 4: how many eligible investors

From the people you already know who meet the eligibility test, estimate a realistic average commitment. Say your best estimate is 200,000 dollars each. Investors needed under route E are 4,000,000 divided by 200,000, which is 20. Now apply a realistic conversion rate. If, from past experience, one in three eligible people you already know who review the documents actually commits, you need 60 qualified reviewers. If your known circle of eligible people is only 35, the raise does not close at this size, and you know it before day one.

Worked example two, using the same numbers. Raise the average ticket to 400,000 dollars and you need only 10 eligible investors and 30 reviewers. The deal now depends on fewer, larger investors, which reduces administration but concentrates risk: if one large investor drops out late, you lose 400,000 dollars at once. Many sponsors set a maximum share any single investor can take, and hold a backstop commitment from a partner or themselves.

Step 5: the compliance budget

Work backward from the investor count. Hypothetical costs: securities counsel 40,000 dollars for the offering structure and documents; eligibility verification at 500 dollars per investor for 20 investors, which is 10,000 dollars; filings and fees of 5,000 dollars; and an accountant's review of the financial information in the offering document, 15,000 dollars. Total 70,000 dollars, or about 1.6 percent of the 4,500,000 dollars raised. That cost belongs in the sources and uses, not in hope.

Step 6: the calendar

Now work backward from day 120, when equity must be in. Funds must clear and be confirmed: allow 10 days, so subscriptions must close by day 110. Investors need time to review documents and take advice: allow 30 days, so documents must be final by day 80. Counsel needs time to structure, draft and review: allow 40 days, so counsel must be engaged by day 40. And before engaging counsel you need a clean pro forma and project description: allow 20 days, so that work must start by day 20. If today is day 0, you have 20 days of slack. Any delay beyond that pushes the raise past the lender's deadline. A buffer belongs at the front, not the end.

Step 7: what the reverse calculation told you

Before speaking to anyone, you now know four things. Route R can carry at most 500,000 dollars, so the deal depends on eligible investors. You need about 20 of them at your expected ticket, and about 60 qualified reviewers. The compliance cost is about 70,000 dollars. And counsel must be engaged by day 40. If any of those does not fit, the right answer is to change the deal, perhaps less leverage or a single institutional partner, not to stretch the exemption.

Step 8: testing the assumptions that drive the answer

Two assumptions decide this calculation: the average ticket and the conversion rate. Run them both ways before you rely on either. If the average ticket falls from 200,000 to 150,000 dollars, eligible investors needed rise from 20 to 4,000,000 divided by 150,000, which is 26.7, so 27. At one in three, that is 81 qualified reviewers. If the conversion rate is one in four rather than one in three, the 20 investors at 200,000 dollars need 80 reviewers. Both moves, together, push the requirement above 100 qualified reviewers, nearly three times your known circle of 35. A raise that looked feasible on the central case fails decisively on modest changes.

That is not a reason to give up. It is a reason to change the shape of the raise before you start. You might seek one or two larger investors who can each take a meaningful share, reduce the equity required by phasing the project, or bring in a single co-investing partner whose capital replaces many small tickets. Each of those options has its own legal and commercial terms to work through with counsel. What you must not do is discover the shortfall on day 100 and start widening the circle in ways the exemption does not permit.

A sensible rule of practice: if the raise only closes on the central case, plan as if it will not. Hold a backstop, or reduce the size, so that the downside case still closes inside the rules.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is starting a raise that cannot close lawfully at its size and on its timetable, and then being tempted to bend the exemption to finish. The control is this reverse calculation, done with counsel's real limits, before any conversation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts interested people. The calculation counts eligible people who will actually commit, inside a capped exemption, on a fixed calendar.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information: implied land price, rent and return. The same habit applies to capital. Start from the finished number, the equity the lender requires, and walk back until each assumption is either confirmed or killed.

Recap

From the equity required, subtract your own; cap the relationship route; size the eligible route by ticket and conversion; price compliance per investor; and set the calendar backward from the lender's deadline. If it does not fit, change the deal, not the rules.

Next: JAX on The Room: the dinner where a friend asks to invest.
checklist: Have I calculated the investor equity required from cost, loan and my own equity?
Do I have counsel's real limits for each exemption route?
Have I calculated the maximum the capped route can carry?
Have I sized the eligible route by realistic ticket and conversion rate?
Is my known eligible circle large enough to close?
Is the compliance budget in sources and uses?
Have I built the calendar backward from the lender's deadline with front-end slack?
head: Field checklist
speak: Start from the finished raise. Hypothetically, a 15,000,000 dollar project with a 65 percent loan needs 5,250,000 dollars of equity; with 750,000 dollars of our own, investors must supply 4,500,000 dollars within 120 days. If, for illustration, a relationship route is capped at 10 investors of 50,000 dollars, it carries at most 500,000 dollars, so 4,000,000 dollars must come from eligible investors. At a 200,000 dollar average ticket that is 20 investors, and at a one-in-three commitment rate, 60 qualified reviewers. If my eligible circle is 35, the raise cannot close at this size. Compliance costs about 70,000 dollars, 1.6 percent. Working backward from day 120, counsel must be engaged by day 40. If it does not fit, I change the deal, not the rules.
terms: Conversion rate — the share of qualified people reviewing an offering who actually commit, estimated from experience.
Backstop commitment — an undertaking by a sponsor or partner to fund any shortfall in a raise.
Concentration limit — a cap on the share of a raise any single investor may take.

hostile.q: You need 4,000,000 dollars from eligible investors in 120 days. What happens if you only find 3,000,000 dollars?
hostile.a: I will know by day 90, not day 119, because the calendar has check-points. If eligible commitments are short, the backstop applies: my partner and I have committed in writing to fund up to 500,000 dollars, and a single institutional investor has agreed terms for a further share. If that still does not close the gap, we resize the project or extend the purchase, rather than relax the exemption.

title: The Dinner Where a Friend Asks to Invest
summary: A realistic scene: at a social dinner, a friend hears about your project and asks to put money in. This lesson is about declining correctly: what to say, what never to say, the question behind his request and how to stay warm without making a statement that breaks securities rules. It teaches restraint, not outreach.
body:
The most dangerous securities conversation is the friendly one you did not plan. When someone asks to invest, your job in that room is to say nothing that counts as an offer, and to move the question to a lawful process later.

Recall

Q. When reverse engineering a raise, why do you cap the relationship route first?

A. Because its limit sets a ceiling on what close contacts can contribute, which tells you how much must come from eligible investors.

Q. What is a deadlock in a partnership?

A. A state where a required decision cannot be made because the partners who must consent will not agree.

Q. Why do banks ask about the source of funds?

A. Because anti-money-laundering rules require them to understand where money came from, and unexplained funds can delay or stop a transaction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will be asked. At a family event, after a presentation, in a car park. Someone you like will say, "If you ever need investors, count me in." The pull is to be generous and say yes. But anything you say about returns, safety or terms can be an offer of a security, can be general solicitation if repeated widely, and can become a misrepresentation if it later proves wrong. This lesson does not teach you how to approach investors. It teaches you how to hold back until the lawful process exists. The scene is hypothetical.

The scene

Dinner at a friend's home. You mention you are working on a building. Another guest leans in: "That sounds great. How much are you looking for? I could do a hundred thousand. What kind of return are we talking about? It's safe, right? Real estate always goes up."

The question behind the question is: "Can I trust you with my money, and will you tell me it is safe?" He is asking for reassurance, not information. Reassurance is exactly what you must not give.

The lines to say

"Thank you, that means a lot. I can't talk about investing in the project tonight. Raising money from anyone has to go through a proper legal process, and I haven't set one up. I'd rather do it properly than casually." Then move the conversation: "Let me tell you what the building is like instead." Describing the design, the neighbourhood or the schedule as a project is different from discussing it as an investment, though once a raise is planned, counsel should tell you what you may say even about that.

If he presses: "I understand. If and when there is an offering, it will only be available to people who qualify under the rules, and it will come with documents and advice. I'm not able to say more than that."

Say that out loud now.

I can't talk about investing tonight; it has to go through a proper legal process.

The lines never to say

Never name a return: not a number, not a range, not "double your money." Never say "safe," "guaranteed," "can't lose" or "real estate always goes up." Never say "I'll put you down for a hundred," which sounds like an allocation. Never say "don't worry about the paperwork." Never discuss other investors or who else is in. Never promise to keep a place for him. Each of these can be read later as an offer, a representation or a promise you did not keep.

When to stay silent

Stay silent rather than correct his claim that real estate always goes up; correcting it invites a discussion of risk and return, which is exactly the investment conversation you are avoiding. A neutral "Every project has risks" is enough, then change the subject. Stay silent about the deal's numbers even if he asks politely more than once. Silence here is not rudeness. It is discipline.

Holding your state

The pressure in this scene is social, not hostile. You will want to be liked, and you may be proud of the project. Notice that pull. Your composure comes from knowing that a "not tonight" protects him as much as you. Before events where the project may come up, decide your one sentence in advance, so you do not improvise.

What happens afterwards

Write a short note that evening: who asked, when, what you said. If you later run a raise, counsel will want to know who you have spoken to, and how, because it can affect which exemption is available. Do not send him anything about the project as an investment. If he contacts you again, the same answer applies until counsel has set up the process, and from then on, only through it.

How the best do it

Disciplined sponsors keep a single rule across their whole team: nobody discusses investment terms outside an approved process, and every enquiry is logged and passed to the person responsible for compliance. A small developer can copy this from day one, even with a team of one: a one-sentence answer, a log, and a rule that investment talk only happens inside counsel's process.

Working with advisers

This month's thread is working with advisers. The friend's question is a reminder that the adviser you need is engaged before the first conversation, not after the first cheque. Give securities counsel a clear instruction: the project, the amount, where likely investors live, and every conversation you have already had.

Then listen. If counsel says a route you wanted is closed, the instruction worked. Paying for a "no" early is far cheaper than paying for a defence later.

If he is offended

Some people will take "not tonight" as a sign you do not trust them. Do not argue the point. Say, simply: "It isn't about you. It's about doing this properly, for everyone, including you. If I ever do raise money, I'd want you to have proper documents and time to take advice." That reframes the refusal as care rather than distance, which is what it is.

If he says, "Come on, I'm not going to sue you," resist the urge to agree. Friendships change, and so do circumstances. The investor who promises never to sue you is the investor who most needs the protection of a proper process, because he is relying entirely on trust. Smile, keep the answer the same, and move on.

And if someone else at the table joins in, "I'd want in too," the risk grows. A table of people hearing about returns is closer to a public pitch than a private chat. Close the subject for everyone with the same sentence, and do not let the evening become a presentation.

None of this requires coldness. You can be warm, interested in his life and generous with your time, while being completely closed on the one subject the law treats as a regulated act. That combination, warmth with a firm boundary, is what people remember as integrity.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a casual reassurance that becomes an offer, a misrepresentation or general solicitation. The control is a prepared one-sentence answer, silence on returns and safety, and a same-day note of the conversation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a friendly chat is not a legal event. To a regulator or a court, what you said about returns and safety can matter as much as what you wrote.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught influence and the pull of liking and social proof. This scene is that pull turned on you: you like him, he likes you, and the easiest thing is to say yes. Knowing the bias is what lets you decline gracefully.

Recap

When someone asks to invest, thank them, say you cannot discuss investing outside a proper legal process, and change the subject. Never name returns, never say safe, never allocate. Log the conversation, and let counsel set the process.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 70's six questions, the Red Pen and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Have I prepared my one-sentence answer before events where the project may come up?
Did I avoid naming any return or range?
Did I avoid the words safe, guaranteed and can't lose?
Did I avoid any allocation or reserved place?
Did I avoid discussing other investors?
Did I log who asked, when and what I said?
Have I given counsel a list of every conversation before any raise?
head: Field checklist
speak: When a friend asks to invest, his real question is whether he can trust me and whether I'll say it is safe. Reassurance is exactly what I must not give. I say: thank you, I can't talk about investing tonight, raising money has to go through a proper legal process and I haven't set one up, I'd rather do it properly. If he presses, I say any offering would only be for people who qualify, with documents and advice. I never name a return, never say safe or guaranteed, never allocate a place, never discuss other investors and never say don't worry about the paperwork. I stay silent rather than debate risk, change the subject to the building as a project, log the conversation that evening, and give counsel the full list of conversations before any raise.
terms: Offer — a communication that invites someone to buy a security, which can arise in conversation as well as in writing.
Misrepresentation — an untrue statement of a material fact, or an omission that makes a statement misleading.
Enquiry log — a record of who asked about investing, when and what was said, kept for counsel and compliance.

hostile.q: Your friend says that at a dinner you told him the project was safe and would pay 15 percent. Did you make him an offer?
hostile.a: No. My note from that evening, written the same night, records that I said I could not discuss investing outside a proper legal process, and that every project has risks. I named no return and made no allocation. When we later ran the offering through counsel, he received the offering document with its risk factors, like every investor, and his eligibility was checked like everyone else's.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 70 Review: Securities, Exemptions and Restraint
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas: the investment contract test, exemptions and their conditions, general solicitation, rescission as a contingent liability, resale restrictions and the reverse-engineered raise. The Red Pen marks up a hypothetical public post, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: taking passive money for a share of your project's profit is usually selling a security, so the exemption, the eligible investors and the permitted channels must be settled with counsel before you say a word.

Recall

Q. What is vesting in a partner agreement?

A. The process by which a partner's share becomes permanent only as defined time or milestone conditions are met.

Q. What is a capital call register?

A. A written record of each capital call notice, payment and remedy election, with dates.

Q. Why do indirect tax concessions need careful records?

A. Because the concession usually depends on conditions, and the business must be able to prove it met them if the tax authority reviews the claim.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, securities law is the area where good intentions protect you least. If you can answer these six questions aloud, you can brief counsel properly, spot a plan going wrong and explain to a lender why your equity is clean. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What makes an interest in a real estate project a security?

Answer: In substance, an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profit from the efforts of others, judged on economic reality, not labels, as in Howey in 1946 and Pacific Coast Coin Exchange in 1978.

Question 2. What is a prospectus exemption, and what must you be able to show?

Answer: A rule permitting sales without a prospectus to defined buyers or on defined conditions. You must be able to prove every condition for every investor, including eligibility, filings and marketing limits.

Question 3. Why can a public post destroy an exemption?

Answer: Because many exemptions forbid or restrict general solicitation, and a public post can be general solicitation for the whole raise.

Question 4. Why does a failed exemption behave like a contingent liability?

Answer: Because it can give investors a right of rescission, called when the project is weakest, which drains liquidity, can trigger a loan default and dilutes other returns.

Question 5. What do resale restrictions mean for investors and for your exit?

Answer: Investors may not be able to sell freely, so they must be told, and your exit and transfer plans cannot assume a liquid market for the interests.

Question 6. How do you reverse engineer a raise?

Answer: Start from the equity required, subtract your own, cap any limited exemption route, size the eligible route by ticket and conversion, price compliance per investor and build the calendar backward from the lender's deadline.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

JAX explained what a security is, why the default is a prospectus and how exemptions and marketing limits work. Ford and Cole took a composite raise that lost its exemption after public posts, giving Rule 70. Roman priced a failed exemption as a contingent liability. REGA set out the three regulatory tests. Sage reverse engineered a raise. JAX ran the dinner where a friend asks to invest.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical public post and find the defects before reading on.

Exciting news! I'm building 20 new homes downtown and opening it up to a few friends and followers. Minimum just 25,000 dollars. Projected 18 percent a year, fully secured by real estate, so your money is safe. Spots are limited and closing Friday. Message me and I'll send the paperwork. No experience needed!

The defects. First, posting publicly to "followers" is very likely general solicitation, which many exemptions forbid. Second, "opening it up" and "message me" is an invitation to buy securities, made before any exemption was confirmed. Third, "projected 18 percent a year" states a return with no basis, assumptions or risks. Fourth, "fully secured" and "your money is safe" are misleading: equity ranks behind the lender and can be lost entirely. Fifth, "spots are limited and closing Friday" is pressure that discourages advice. Sixth, a low minimum with "no experience needed" suggests investors will not be checked for eligibility. Seventh, there is no mention of risks, resale restrictions, conflicts or the offering document. And eighth, nobody qualified approved it: there is no sign counsel saw it.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why can't we just raise from people we know?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because what we would be selling is a security. Passive investors putting money into our project, expecting profit from our work, is the classic investment contract. The default rule is that securities sold to the public need a prospectus, which is too slow and costly for us, so we rely on exemptions. Each exemption has conditions: who may buy, how much, which documents, what filings, and limits on marketing. We have to prove every condition for every investor, and the rules follow where each investor lives. If we get it wrong, investors may be able to demand their money back, usually when the project is under pressure, and the lender can freeze the loan. So we engage securities counsel first, work backward from the equity we need to see whether our eligible circle can fill it, verify every investor, and say nothing about investing to anyone until the process is set up."

Score yourself: did you name the investment contract test? Did you explain exemptions as conditions to prove? Did you mention marketing limits and rescission? Did you finish in two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

How the post should have been handled

There is no compliant version of that post for this course to write, because the right answer is not a better post. The right answer is no post at all until securities counsel has designed the raise. If counsel later concludes that an exemption permitting some form of public communication is available, the wording, the channels, the investor verification steps and the disclosures will come from counsel and the rules, not from the developer's enthusiasm. That is the discipline Rule 70 enforces: the first communication is a legal act, and it is drafted by someone qualified to draft it.

Notice too that every defect in the post is a defect of over-reassurance: safe, secured, projected, limited, no experience needed. The instinct that produces those words is a sales instinct, and it is a good instinct when selling a finished apartment to a buyer who will live in it. It is the wrong instinct when selling a share of an unfinished project to a passive investor who cannot inspect it. Learn to hear the difference in your own voice.

A useful habit for the drill: read the post aloud and, after each sentence, ask whether you could prove it with a document today. Every sentence you cannot prove is a defect, and most of this post fails that test.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is speaking or posting about an investment before the exemption is fixed. The control is Rule 70: counsel's written confirmation of the exemption, investors, channels and documents before any communication.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that small amounts or friendly investors take a raise outside securities law. They change which exemption may apply; they rarely remove the law.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught that substance beats form in tax: the label on a transaction does not decide how it is treated. Securities law runs on the same principle. Calling investors "partners" does not make their interests anything other than what the economics say they are.

Recap

Passive profit-sharing interests are usually securities. Private raises rely on exemptions whose conditions must be proved investor by investor. Marketing limits, rescission risk and resale restrictions shape the raise. Reverse engineer it, verify it and keep quiet until counsel has built the process.

Next: JAX, with Nadia, on First Principles: the offering document, and why every word in it can be sued on.
checklist: What makes an interest in a real estate project a security?
What is a prospectus exemption, and what must you be able to show?
Why can a public post destroy an exemption?
Why does a failed exemption behave like a contingent liability?
What do resale restrictions mean for investors and for your exit?
How do you reverse engineer a raise?
head: The six questions
speak: Passive money in a common enterprise, expecting profit from my efforts, is usually a security, judged on substance as in Howey and Pacific Coast Coin Exchange. Selling to the public needs a prospectus, so private raises rely on exemptions, and I must prove every condition for every investor: eligibility, filings, documents and marketing limits, under the rules where each investor lives. A public post can be general solicitation and destroy the exemption. A failed exemption can create a rescission right, a contingent liability called when the project is weakest, which can freeze the loan. Private securities usually carry resale restrictions, so investors must be told and my exit cannot assume liquidity. I reverse engineer the raise from the equity required, and when anyone asks to invest before the process exists, I decline. Rule 70: counsel confirms the exemption, investors, channels and documents in writing before any communication.
terms: Issuer — the person or entity that creates and sells a security, usually the vehicle that will own the project.
Risk acknowledgement — a document some exemptions require an investor to sign, confirming it understands it may lose its investment.
Hold period — a period after a private sale during which the securities cannot be freely resold.

hostile.q: A screenshot shows you posted about returns of 18 percent to your followers. How is your exemption still valid?
hostile.a: If that post is mine, it may not be, and I would not argue otherwise. I have asked securities counsel to assess its effect on the exemption, and I will not close the raise until that is answered. If the exemption is compromised, the options are regulatory guidance, a fresh compliant offering, or not accepting those investors, and any cost of curing it will come from capital outside the project.
